reading the word directory out of the sentence wins over guessing, because the cp rule already did exactly that
consulting the existing side-effecting-flag table wins over a new list, because the table was already maintained
comparing two real directory trees wins over comparing answer strings, because a mutation is a promise about files

Intercepting the adapter call showed test_paths bound to three entries for a sentence that names three paths in three roles: the source root directory, the one real test, and the output report. challenger_routes.why_not_selected_or_selected: SELECTED: a previous guard already dropped the output path, but only by recognising an output VERB, and this sentence says 'save output_path R.json' with no 'to', so the guard never fired -- and nothing at all excluded the source root. Enumerating another verb would fix one phrasing and leave the class. The general rule is role exclusivity: a repository path named in a sentence has exactly one role, so any path already bound to another input key is not also a member of a *_paths list. challenger_routes.why_not_selected_or_selected: SELECTED: apply the gate that already exists to the fallback before it may report success. Two supporting defects were found by measuring the same family. (1) Template key order for the repair capabilities is output_path, source_root, test_argv, test_paths, and test_argv is derived FROM the test paths, so counting a derived argv as a competing claim cancelled the role against itself: exclusivity emptied a correct test_paths, the fallback then assigned every file in the sentence, source included. route_frontier.negative_search_summary: Ordinary POSIX commands need no external package.  The live challengers were to add an append capability to the registry -- rejected because it adds a producer to trust where a command and a postcondition suffice -- to use `sed -e` with a write-back, rejected on measurement because an append is not idempotent and the re-run check refused the correct file, and to put sed in the mutating table for every shape, rejected because it would route every sed reading away from the check that judges it.

mv into directory destination is a directory postcondition
rm -r recursive delete verification file system state

BROAD_WEB_OR_COMMUNITY: https://api.github.com/search/repositories?q=postcondition%20verify%20effect%20not%20rerun -- a mutating command is verified by the state it left, never by running it twice; no standalone project owns the rule because it is a property of the check
CODE_OR_PACKAGE_REGISTRY: https://pypi.org/pypi/astunparse/json and the standard library's own compile() error handling -- both treat a parse failure as a property of one input rather than a fatal condition for the caller

recursive_obs.why_selected_route_is_fastest_sufficient: Every one of the four needed a promise stated, not a mechanism invented: sed already appends, `mv` already moves into a directory, `rm -r` already removes a tree, and the postcondition table already held five examples of asking the disk instead of re-running.  The dominant alternative -- adding an append capability to the registry -- loses because it adds a producer to trust where a command and a postcondition already suffice.  The second, `sed -e` with a write-back, loses on measurement: an append is not idempotent, so the re-run check returned COMMAND_OUTPUT_NOT_REPRODUCED over the correct file.  The third, adding sed to the mutating table for every shape, loses because it would route every sed reading away from the re-run check that judges it.
